mcqs.question: Why can a shared rate limiter need to sustain higher QPS than any single service it protects?
options: It doesn't — the limiter's QPS always matches its busiest protected service
Because it aggregates checks across every service that calls it, so total check volume can exceed any one service's own traffic
Because rate limiting requires 10x more compute per request than normal processing
Because the limiter must also handle each service's business logic
mcqs.explanation: A shared limiter is called by every protected service, so its total check volume is the sum across all of them, which can dwarf any single service's own QPS. It doesn't run business logic, and there's no inherent 10x compute multiplier for a rate-limit check itself.

mcqs.question: Why do per-node in-memory counters undercount actual request rates for a rate limiter?
options: In-memory counters overflow at low values
A client's requests get load-balanced across multiple limiter instances, each of which only sees its own partial share of that client's traffic
In-memory storage cannot support atomic increments
Per-node counters are always slower than a shared store
mcqs.explanation: If a client's requests land on different limiter instances, each instance's local counter only reflects the slice of traffic it personally saw, undercounting the true total — a shared store avoids this by being the one source of truth. In-memory counters don't overflow at normal limiter values, do support atomic increments, and are actually faster than a shared store, not slower.

mcqs.question: Why must rate limits live in a config store the limiter reads dynamically, rather than being hardcoded in the deployed service?
options: Hardcoded limits are technically impossible to implement
Requirements state limits must change without a redeploy of any consuming service
Dynamic config is always faster to read than hardcoded values
It is required for the checkAndIncrement operation to be atomic
mcqs.explanation: The non-functional requirement that limits change without redeploying consumers is exactly why config must live somewhere the limiter can read and refresh dynamically. Hardcoding is technically possible, just doesn't meet that requirement; reading from a config store isn't inherently faster, and atomicity of the increment operation is unrelated to where config values live.

mcqs.question: Why do most production rate limiters accept relaxed, per-node approximate enforcement instead of strict global accuracy?
options: Approximate enforcement is required by most cloud providers
Strict accuracy is impossible to implement with any shared store
A caller occasionally exceeding a soft quota by a small margin is a cheaper failure than making the limiter a platform-wide bottleneck or single point of failure
Approximate limits use less network bandwidth than strict ones
mcqs.explanation: The real trade-off is availability and latency versus perfect enforcement — occasionally letting a caller slightly exceed its quota is a minor cost compared to the limiter itself becoming a bottleneck for every protected service. Strict accuracy is achievable with a shared store, just costlier; there's no cloud-provider mandate, and bandwidth isn't the deciding factor here.

mcqs.question: Your rate limiter service becomes unreachable. What should the calling services do by default?
options: Block all requests until the limiter recovers, to guarantee no limit is ever exceeded
Retry the limiter call indefinitely with no timeout
Fail open or fall back to an approximate local decision, rather than making the limiter's availability the ceiling for the entire platform
Permanently disable rate limiting for that caller going forward
mcqs.explanation: Blocking on limiter unavailability turns a shared utility's outage into a company-wide outage — an explicit fail-open or approximate-fallback path is the safer default, trading temporarily relaxed enforcement for platform-wide availability. Indefinite retries just delay the same failure, and permanently disabling limiting removes protection long after the incident ends.
